chapter: Mahalia Jackson concert and Congo Square
title: Turned away from the Mahalia Jackson concert
summary: In 1957-58 Wood and his wife were stopped by a policeman at the Municipal Auditorium, argued with the manager, and Bill Russell tried the stage door without success.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: We've talked so much about the brass bands. Tell me about going to here in my hair, Joe. Oh, okay.

Yeah. You did want to make sure. Well, again, I don't remember exactly what year that was. It was, my guess is it was 58, but it might have been 57. But I remember that I first became aware of it when riding on the Fred Street bus and seeing notices on telephone poles and in record shops, placards, that she was going to be here. And so I, you know, we might have not talked about it. We certainly would like to go and hear her do that. And so we made our plans to do so. She was going to sing on a Sunday, I believe, at the Municipal Auditorium. And we went down early because we had not bought tickets ahead of time and had to stand in a long line. We were two white faces in a great sea of black people that were waiting to buy tickets and got up to the ticket window and bought tickets. I was thinking about this a couple of days ago that I don't remember what they cost, but I do remember they were expensive. You know, that I felt like I was, as a graduate student, didn't have much cash money and that I was making a special effort to buy those more. It was costing me. It cost a hell of a lot more than going to a movie or something, you know. It was a big expenditure. And so we bought our tickets and went on into the building. And there's a black man there who took our tickets up and greeted us cordially and said, Come on in, white folks, sit anywhere you like. And we went on in and got another 50 feet. And the white New Orleans policeman grabbed me by the arm and said, You know, where do you think you're going? And I said, Well, I want to go in here to hear Bahia Jackson sing. And he said, You can't come in here. And so I remonstrated with him a little bit and went, you know, it was pretty clear that he wasn't going to let us in. And you say you don't remember this, but about that time you came walking by following in the wake of some black woman who had a ribbon on it that said committee. And you were carrying an arm load of what looked like printed programs for the occasion. And by that time it was clear I was going to be thrown out. And I thought, Aha, how clever Dick Allen is that he has gotten in by assuming this official role in the service of the committee woman. But the policeman let me go back to the box office to get my money back. But then I thought more and thought, Well, I want to talk to the manager. So we went to the manager's office. And by the time we got there, there were six or eight other white people there who also had been thrown out. And there are various states of anger. Everybody is yelling at the manager of the place. About that time you appeared in the manager's office. And Bill Russell was there by then too. Some people were just sort of quietly trying to persuade the guy to let him in after all. And others were denouncing the whole system and claiming their constitutional rights and threatening lawsuits. And the manager was just saying, I have no control over it whatsoever. The promoters are the ones. And if they will designate an area for white people to sit in, we can let you in. But they have not set aside a space for white people. And you can't go in until they do. And so we eventually got somebody who was a promoter or the promoter's assistant to come over there and talk to us. And he again reiterated his welcome and said, we're just delighted to have you. Come sit anywhere you want to. But he would not designate a special section of the auditorium for white people. And as much as I wanted to hear Mahalia Jackson sing, I admired his stand on it. And he wasn't going to be bullied and shoved down. And so the manager just refused to let us in. And Bill Russell gathered you and I think Ida and I followed along with you. And I think Irvin Helfer was there too, as I think back on that.

And it was just that tiny little night. There was not all the white people who were in the manager's office who went out with Bill Russell. And he said, we'll go around and see if we can't go in the stage door and stand in the wings. And he knew Mahalia Jackson or she knew him. They were acquainted well. And his idea was that he would get permission for him and his friends to come in and stand in the wings and hear us sing. So we went back to the stage door and hung around outside and messages went in and out. And finally her brother came out and spoke to us. And somebody told me he was her brother. And he apparently lived in New Orleans and she was living in Chicago by that time, I think. And he was kind of a ne'er-do-well, I gather. But he became a messenger. He at first was reluctant to even take the message in to his sister from Bill Russell because he didn't want to upset her. But finally he did take a message in. And all of that was to no avail. At one point he came out and said that he had brought the message from Mahalia Jackson that it hurt her in the heart that Bill Russell and her friends couldn't hear her sing in New Orleans. But we finally gave up and went away. Walked back down to Morning Call and had a cup of coffee and some beignets. And I felt very much discriminated against. It's the only time in my life that I remember being discriminated against by the color of my skin. And the black promoter certainly struck a blow for integration with me, the way you handled the whole thing.
